3. Cross-year requirements on the source

source-requirements.Rmd

Every rule in the previous tutorial is a statement about rows you already have. state = "GA" can be checked one row at a time; so can filter_501c = "3". apply_sfw() evaluates them against a data frame and that is the end of it.

Some sampling criteria are not like that:

Which organizations filed in all three of 2019, 2020 and 2021?

Which were 990EZ filers every year, never switching to the full 990?

Neither question can be answered from a single row, or even from a single table-year. They are facts about the source. Worse, the obvious way to answer them — build the panel, then filter it — reads exactly the data you were hoping to avoid reading. You download three years of every column to discover that you wanted 5,560 organizations out of 241,552.

A require rule states such a condition, and resolve_frame() answers it against the source before the real read happens.

Declaring a requirement

require is a rule type like any other, so it goes on the frame the same way:

frame <- create_sfw("balanced 990EZ filers", record = "OBJECTID")
frame <- add_rule(frame, "balanced", type = "require", present_in = "all")
frame <- add_rule(frame, "always_ez", type = "require", present_in = "any",
                  column = "RETURN_TYPE", op = "in", values = "990EZ",
                  holds = "every")
get_rules(frame)
#>        name    type active                                               detail
#> 1  balanced require   TRUE                                  P00: present in all
#> 2 always_ez require   TRUE P00: present in any; every year RETURN_TYPE in 990EZ

Two arguments carry the cross-year meaning:

present_in — how many of the requested years the organization must appear in. "all" (the default) gives a balanced frame, "any" imposes no presence requirement, and an integer sets a minimum: present_in = 2 accepts anything observed in at least two years.

holds — how a per-filing predicate folds over the years. "every" (the default) requires RETURN_TYPE == "990EZ" in every year observed; "any" requires it in at least one. The predicate itself is the ordinary structured column/op/values triple used by filter rules.

The two combine, so present_in and holds are independent choices:

present_in holds Reads as
"all" "every" in every year, and a 990EZ filer in each
"any" "every" a 990EZ filer in every year it did file
"all" "any" in every year, and a 990EZ filer at least once

An expr string is refused rather than quietly ignored, because an opaque predicate cannot be pushed to the source:

add_rule(frame, type = "require", expr = "RETURN_TYPE == '990EZ'")
#> Error in `.sfw_require_payload()`:
#> ! `require` rules need a structured `column`/`op`/`values` predicate; an `expr` string cannot be pushed to the source.

Resolving against the source

resolve_frame() executes the requirements and rewrites the frame:

frame <- resolve_frame(frame, years = 2009:2011,
                       source = data_source(format = "parquet"))
#> <- REQUIRE  balanced [F9-P00-T00-HEADER x 3 year(s)]: 33,946 EIN2 in 0.04s
#> <- REQUIRE  always_ez [F9-P00-T00-HEADER x 3 year(s)]: 94,422 EIN2 in 0.06s
#> resolve_frame: 5,560 EIN2 satisfy 2 requirement(s).

Multiple requirements intersect: an organization must satisfy all of them. 33,946 organizations filed in all three years, and 94,422 never filed anything other than a 990EZ — 5,560 satisfy both.

What comes back is an ordinary frame whose sample is now concrete:

get_rules(frame)
#>        name    type active                                               detail
#> 1  balanced require  FALSE                                  P00: present in all
#> 2 always_ez require  FALSE P00: present in any; every year RETURN_TYPE in 990EZ
#> 3  resolved  subset   TRUE                                             5560 ids

The requirements are deactivated, not dropped, and the answer arrives as a captured subset rule. That is the whole design:

  • The frame stays declarative and source-agnostic. apply_sfw() never learns about years or files — it only ever sees a subset, which it already knows how to execute against any data frame.
  • The sample is reproducible and auditable. The ids are captured by value, and the frame still records the question next to the answer.

manifest() logs the resolution, so a panel built this way explains where its sample came from:

manifest(frame)
#>                step                                               detail rows_after
#> 1  require: balanced                                  P00: present in all      33946
#> 2 require: always_ez P00: present in any; every year RETURN_TYPE in 990EZ      94422
#> 3      resolve_frame                         2 requirement(s) intersected       5560

Why it is cheap

Resolution reads the entity key, the time key, and any column a predicate names — nothing else. The financial columns are never touched, because the question does not involve them.

On a parquet release that is two or three columns of one table. Answering “who filed in all three years” over the 2009–2011 header table reads 1.4 MB of EIN2 and TAX_YEAR. The same three files as CSV are 273 MB, and a CSV scan has to read all of it because a text file has no column boundaries to seek to.

# Both resolve to the same 5,560 ids.
data_source(format = "parquet")   # 0.17s
data_source(format = "csv")       # 1.10s locally, far worse over the network

The requirement is answered the same way on either format — resolve_frame() works on a CSV release too. Parquet just makes it nearly free, and the gap widens without a local cache, where column pruning becomes a handful of HTTP range requests instead of a whole-file transfer. See data_source() for the format’s type contract.

Handing it to panelize()

panelize() resolves an outstanding requirement on its own, before the read it is meant to narrow:

panel <- panelize(
  frame, tables = c("P00", "P01"), years = 2009:2011,
  source  = data_source(format = "parquet"),
  backend = "duckdb",       # pushes the subset into the scan
  cache   = "none",         # read the published files in place
  unique_rows = FALSE       # let the column projection reach the scan
)

There is no need to call resolve_frame() first — the frame above would work passed straight to panelize(). Resolving it by hand is useful when you want to inspect the sample, reuse one id set across several builds, or pin it for reproducibility.

The three acquisition arguments are what turn the resolved subset into a narrow read rather than a filter after the fact. unique_rows = FALSE matters more than it looks: deduplication compiles to SELECT DISTINCT *, which needs every column and so blocks the projection from reaching the scan. The efile build emits no exact duplicate rows, so switching it off is both faster and equivalent.

Coverage is not one row per year

A requirement guarantees that an organization appears in each year. It does not guarantee one row per year, because an amended return is a second filing for the same tax year:

table(table(panel_data(panel)$EIN2))
#>    3    4    5
#> 5508   49    3

That is a different job, and there is already a rule for it. Add a dedup rule and each organization-year collapses to one filing:

panel <- panelize(add_rule(frame, type = "dedup"), tables = c("P00", "P01"),
                  years = 2009:2011, source = data_source(format = "parquet"),
                  backend = "duckdb", cache = "none", unique_rows = FALSE)
table(table(panel_data(panel)$EIN2))
#>    3
#> 5560

Keep the two concerns separate: require decides who is in the sample, dedup decides which filing represents an organization-year. See deduplicate() for how the winning filing is chosen.

Choosing between require and filter

A filter rule is the right tool whenever the criterion can be read off one row. Reach for require only when the condition spans years:

Criterion Rule
filed a 990EZ this year filter on RETURN_TYPE
a 990EZ filer every year require, holds = "every"
in Georgia filter on geo_state_abbr (BMF)
present in all requested years require, present_in = "all"
observed at least twice require, present_in = 2

require also overlaps with panel_balance(), and the difference is when the work happens. panel_balance() balances a panel you have already built; require resolves the balanced sample first and never reads the rows it is going to drop. Use panel_balance() when the panel is already in memory, and require when you are about to acquire it.
